constraints: The screen reader must distinguish both controls and the revision each action targets; revision attribution is maintained separately.
A shared editor shows an edit control and a comment anchored to a selected revision.

feedback.reason: A revision-bearing action name associates the control itself with the anchor; it must be refreshed when the selected anchor changes.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The action name is exposed on the control, so a screen-reader user hears which revision that specific Comment button targets.
details.scenarioApplication: Each anchor has a distinct Comment control named for its current revision; when collaboration moves the anchor, the accessible name changes with it.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A nearby revision heading helps orient reading, but it does not associate multiple Comment controls with their individual targets.
details.errorCorrection: Use a distinct name such as “Comment on revision 42” on the control attached to revision 42, and update it if that anchor moves.
details.transfer: When a list contains repeated actions, include the item context in each action name and keep that context synchronized with the item.

messages.text: A visible nearby label may be skipped or detached from the particular Comment control when the page has several anchors.
The opening revision can change during collaboration; retaining it in the name would identify yesterday’s target.
A toolbar name identifies the group, but not which revision each repeated Comment action affects.

options.text: Name both actions clearly and place the revision beside the anchor as visible context.
Include the selected revision in the comment name when the editor first opens.
Use one named editor toolbar and expose the selected text as the action context.
Give each Comment action a name containing its current revision anchor.

prompt: A shared editor shows an edit control and a comment anchored to a selected revision. The screen reader must distinguish both controls and the revision each action targets; revision attribution is maintained separately. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: Assistive technology must identify the signed revision, while a separate service verifies provenance and authorization.
A signing page displays the exact document revision awaiting signature.

feedback.reason: A control name can identify which revision the action refers to, but it cannot prove that the transaction is authorized or bound to that revision.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Semantic headings and an action name communicate the document context; cryptographic provenance remains a distinct transaction responsibility.
details.scenarioApplication: The page exposes the revision identifier to the user before activation and the signing service binds the result to that exact revision.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A shorter button label is acceptable when a nearby programmatic relationship provides the revision context; the server still validates provenance.
details.errorCorrection: Name the button “Sign” and rely on the nearby visual revision badge to identify the document. A control name can identify which revision the action refers to, but it cannot prove that the transaction is authorized or bound to that revision.
details.transfer: When a document revision changes, update the accessible context and independently bind the signed result to the verified revision.

messages.text: A name communicates intent but cannot authorize or bind a signature transaction.
A heading alone can be missed when several revisions or actions are present.
Without a programmatic relationship, nearby visual text may not identify the action target.

options.text: Include the revision in Sign’s accessible name and trust that name as the authorization check.
Use a revision heading and a generic Sign action without relating the two.
Name the revision before signing; let the service verify and bind the signature.
Name Sign and show the exact revision in a nearby visual badge.

prompt: A signing page displays the exact document revision awaiting signature. Assistive technology must identify the signed revision, while a separate service verifies provenance and authorization. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: The technician must keep entered notes and still attach a photo using a keyboard-operable fallback.
A field technician captures a site photo; camera permission may be denied after the form is partly completed.

feedback.reason: The draft remains repairable, the failure is explained, and file selection does not depend on camera permission.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A labeled file input is a separate user-operable path; preserving form state avoids turning a permission failure into lost work.
details.scenarioApplication: The technician can retain notes, understand why capture failed, and choose an existing image through the same form.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Retrying camera permission can be offered, but it should not replace a file-selection route when camera access is unavailable.
details.errorCorrection: On denial, clear the draft and restart the capture screen so the camera permission prompt can be retried. The draft remains repairable, the failure is explained, and file selection does not depend on camera permission.
details.transfer: If camera permission is restored, retain the same draft and make capture available alongside file selection.

messages.text: A status explains failure but does not provide an alternative attachment path.
A camera retry may help, but it does not add a photo when permission stays denied.
A server save may lag behind recent notes and cannot stand in for preserving the active draft.

options.text: Keep the camera control and expose permission denial as a textual status.
Keep the draft and offer a labeled file picker when camera access is denied.
Retain the form and offer another camera permission request before adding a file.
Offer file selection after denial and rebuild the form from its last server save.

prompt: A field technician captures a site photo; camera permission may be denied after the form is partly completed. The technician must keep entered notes and still attach a photo using a keyboard-operable fallback. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: The submitted form can contain several errors across separate sections, and users need to review the complete set before choosing one to fix.
Each localized error must identify its field and explain the accepted format; the user can return from the overview to that control.

feedback.reason: A multi-section overview lets the user choose among all reported failures; linked field errors then provide the local format guidance for the selected repair.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A summary that names each invalid control and links to it exposes the full validation result while preserving a direct route to the field-level instruction.
details.scenarioApplication: The user can scan errors across all three sections, choose a field, follow its link, and hear the localized expected format beside that control.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: For one isolated error, direct focus can be efficient. Here, focusing one field first hides the other failures the user needs to compare.
details.errorCorrection: After submit, focus an error summary listing each invalid field; link every entry to its control and associate the localized format message with that control.
details.transfer: When validation is asynchronous, preserve input and announce the final result only after the server response.

messages.text: Focusing one field gives a repair destination, but it withholds the overview needed to choose among errors in three sections.
Field messages help local repair, but without a summary the user lacks an overview after multi-section submit.
A generic alert does not identify the field or accepted format.

options.text: Link localized errors to their fields and focus the summary after submit.
Focus the first invalid field and link its localized format message to the control.
Associate each localized error with its field and omit the multi-section summary.
Focus a generic error alert and leave each field’s label and format unchanged.

prompt: After submission, a registration form reports errors in three sections. The user needs an overview to choose which error to fix, then must understand the localized format and reach that field. Which interface decision supports that repair path?

constraints: Keyboard and screen-reader users must operate the variant control and understand whether a participant was exposed.
An experiment dashboard lets analysts enable an accessible variant and inspect exposure status.

feedback.reason: A control state describes the analyst’s setting; participant exposure is a separate outcome and must not be inferred from it.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Native toggle semantics expose the selected setting, while the exposure status reports what actually happened.
details.scenarioApplication: The analyst can operate the variant control from the keyboard and read exposure data independently of the toggle state.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Exposure may be summarized in a table when the row and column headers identify each cohort; the control still needs its own state.
details.errorCorrection: Give each variant selector an accessible name that identifies its experiment, and report measured participant exposure separately.
details.transfer: If rollout delivery lags behind the setting, announce the cohort’s measured exposure rather than the configured value.

messages.text: The cohort table can explain exposure, but an unlabeled selector gives keyboard and screen-reader users no experiment-specific control name.
Color does not identify which cohort was exposed.
Assignment and exposure can differ during rollout; one checked state collapses them.

options.text: Use a named cohort table for exposure, but leave each row’s variant selector unlabeled.
Show assignment by toggle and exposure through a cohort color in the table.
Separate the labeled assignment control from measured participant exposure.
Use the toggle’s checked state to report both configured variant and exposure.

prompt: An experiment dashboard lets analysts enable an accessible variant and inspect exposure status. Keyboard and screen-reader users must operate the variant control and understand whether a participant was exposed. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: A keyboard or screen-reader user must select a route and read its directions even when the map stalls.
A low-end tablet map has a slow canvas, but route search and selection must remain usable.

feedback.reason: The named canvas does not provide selectable route controls or directions; the semantic list preserves the task without depending on map rendering.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A route list is the task interface; the canvas is a second visualization that can be slow or unavailable.
details.scenarioApplication: The route remains selectable and understandable while the map is loading, and users can still open a selected route’s directions.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A map can remain the fastest path for pointer users, provided the same route choice and details exist in the list.
details.errorCorrection: Label the canvas and its pins, then keep route selection in the map so the same data is not repeated. The named canvas does not provide selectable route controls or directions; the semantic list preserves the task without depending on map rendering.
details.transfer: When canvas performance improves, retain the semantic list for users and devices that cannot use the map interaction.

messages.text: The route list must also support selection; the canvas name alone is not a route alternative.
Pins still depend on canvas output and do not expose the full direction sequence.
On a slow tablet, map rendering can block the route task.

options.text: Name the canvas and provide a separate route list for reading directions.
Make pins keyboard-focusable and let them select a route while the canvas is ready.
Render the map first, then expose route names and directions after it finishes.
Keep a keyboard-selectable route list available without the map canvas.

prompt: A low-end tablet map has a slow canvas, but route search and selection must remain usable. A keyboard or screen-reader user must select a route and read its directions even when the map stalls. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: Users must understand each filter group and reproduce the same filter state from a shared link.
A saved search has filters that must be shareable through a URL.

feedback.reason: A shareable URL preserves state across sessions, while labels and fieldset legends make each filter understandable and operable.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Native form controls and named groups provide semantics; the URL owns reproducible state independently from transient component state.
details.scenarioApplication: Opening the copied URL restores the same filters, and each control retains its own visible and programmatic label.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A local store can cache current edits, but it should not be the only source when the user expects a shareable view.
details.errorCorrection: Use a labeled form but keep selections only in a global store that is not restored from the link. A shareable URL preserves state across sessions, while labels and fieldset legends make each filter understandable and operable.
details.transfer: When filters change, update the URL without changing the group names or labels used to operate them.

messages.text: An unnamed group leaves the purpose of each filter set unclear.
A session store does not reproduce the view when another user opens the link.
Placeholder text is not a persistent label during entry.

options.text: Use native labels but put all filter types in one unnamed group.
Label and group filters; serialize committed selections in the URL.
Use labeled filter groups and keep all selections in a session store.
Serialize filters in the URL and use placeholders as their field names.

prompt: A saved search has filters that must be shareable through a URL. Users must understand each filter group and reproduce the same filter state from a shared link. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: A keyboard user needs an equivalent move action and a clear announcement if another user changes the card first.
A collaborative board supports moving cards by drag; concurrent edits can change a card’s column.

feedback.reason: Focusable drag handles do not create a keyboard move operation; a named move control offers equivalent action and can report a stale target.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A move menu expresses the same intent without pointer dragging, while conflict feedback reports whether that intent was applied.
details.scenarioApplication: The user can move a card using controls and receives a status identifying the final column or the concurrent change.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Drag can remain as a shortcut when the same move is possible through a non-drag control.
details.errorCorrection: Add keyboard focus to draggable cards but keep movement available only through pointer dragging. Focusable drag handles do not create a keyboard move operation; a named move control offers equivalent action and can report a stale target.
details.transfer: When the board reconnects, preserve pending intent and announce whether the server accepted or conflicted with the move.

messages.text: Focus on a handle does not provide an equivalent move operation by itself.
A stale destination can overwrite another user’s accepted move.
A full event replay can obscure the one conflict that affects the user’s pending action.

options.text: Offer a keyboard move action and report whether a concurrent move won.
Give the drag handle keyboard focus and keep the same drag-only gesture.
Offer a move menu but apply its destination without checking a concurrent update.
Expose a keyboard move action and announce every board event after reconnect.

prompt: A collaborative board supports moving cards by drag; concurrent edits can change a card’s column. A keyboard user needs an equivalent move action and a clear announcement if another user changes the card first. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: Assistive technology users need the upload state, while embedded third-party scripts must not read the protected data.
A confidential upload form contains protected fields and a progress indicator.

feedback.reason: DOM naming does not establish a security boundary; access isolation must be enforced separately from the user-facing status.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Labels and status text serve the user; origin or component isolation protects the data from scripts.
details.scenarioApplication: The user can identify upload progress while the sensitive field values remain outside the third-party script’s readable boundary.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A same-origin policy may help with cross-origin scripts, but trusted scripts still need controlled access to protected values.
details.errorCorrection: Place the fields in a named landmark and assume the landmark prevents scripts from reading them. DOM naming does not establish a security boundary; access isolation must be enforced separately from the user-facing status.
details.transfer: If the upload is delegated to a separate origin, expose its result through a narrowly scoped status message.

messages.text: Landmark semantics do not restrict script access to DOM values.
The status can remain accessible without exposing field data to an untrusted script.
Same-origin scripts can still access shared page data unless a separate boundary limits them.

options.text: Place protected fields in a named landmark that the preview script cannot inspect.
Keep the upload status out of the accessibility tree while protecting fields with script isolation.
Expose progress and allow any same-origin script to read protected values.
Expose upload progress; isolate protected fields from third-party scripts.

prompt: A confidential upload form contains protected fields and a progress indicator. Assistive technology users need the upload state, while embedded third-party scripts must not read the protected data. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: The page must expose the correct language and text direction while fitting expanded labels and locale-specific plural forms.
A translated checkout supports Arabic item names and pluralized quantities.

feedback.reason: Direction alone does not select plural categories or prevent mixed-direction text from reordering; locale formatting and flexible layout remain required.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Language, base direction, bidi isolation, plural formatting, and expansion address separate localization behaviors.
details.scenarioApplication: Arabic labels render with correct direction and quantity grammar, while long translations can wrap without clipping.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A component may inherit the page language when it contains no language change; a mixed-language name needs its own boundary.
details.errorCorrection: Set dir=rtl on the page and concatenate an English singular/plural suffix for every item count. Direction alone does not select plural categories or prevent mixed-direction text from reordering; locale formatting and flexible layout remain required.
details.transfer: When a user switches locale, update language and direction metadata as well as formatted values and layout.

messages.text: Mixed-direction values still need appropriate isolation.
Clipping expanded text hides the translated label.
Direction does not select plural forms, and global RTL can misorder embedded identifiers.

options.text: Use locale plural formatting and leave mixed-direction identifiers unisolated.
Set the language and clip expanded labels to preserve fixed English widths.
Set language and direction, format plurals by locale, and allow expansion.
Set right-to-left direction globally and concatenate a translated singular or plural suffix.

prompt: A translated checkout supports Arabic item names and pluralized quantities. The page must expose the correct language and text direction while fitting expanded labels and locale-specific plural forms. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: The user must locate invalid fields and distinguish submission failure from an accepted application.
A permit application can fail server validation after the user submits several sections.

feedback.reason: The server rejection must not look like acceptance; linked summary and field errors support correction while preserving entered data.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The semantic error structure communicates repair targets, and the authoritative result remains an explicit server state.
details.scenarioApplication: The applicant can review all errors, jump to a field, and see that the application remains unsubmitted until accepted.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A client can validate obvious formatting early, but it cannot announce final acceptance before the server confirms it.
details.errorCorrection: Show an error summary but keep the submit button’s “Submitted” label after the server rejects the application. The server rejection must not look like acceptance; linked summary and field errors support correction while preserving entered data.
details.transfer: After resubmission, replace the prior error state with the actual authoritative outcome.

messages.text: Color and an external result do not establish which field needs correction.
Field errors do not correct the misleading accepted state after a server rejection.
Serial focus jumps interrupt repair and remove the overview before all errors are understood.

options.text: Show the server result outside the form and mark invalid fields only by color.
Link server errors to fields and announce the authoritative submission result.
Show linked field errors but leave the submit button labeled “Submitted” after rejection.
Move focus through every invalid field and remove the summary as the user corrects them.

prompt: A permit application can fail server validation after the user submits several sections. The user must locate invalid fields and distinguish submission failure from an accepted application. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: Users must navigate lesson sections and control playback without confusing browser playback state with server lesson metadata.
A course player has lesson landmarks and media controls; playback state is local to the browser.

feedback.reason: Browser playback state cannot prove server completion; a labeled outline and native media controls address the actual interaction.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Native media controls provide established keyboard operation, while lesson structure provides navigable context.
details.scenarioApplication: A learner can navigate the lesson outline, control playback, and separately read whether completion was recorded.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A custom media control is viable when it fully exposes state and keyboard behavior; native controls reduce that implementation burden.
details.errorCorrection: Use a video element with controls but put the lesson outline in an unlabeled sidebar. Browser playback state cannot prove server completion; a labeled outline and native media controls address the actual interaction.
details.transfer: When playback resumes on another device, preserve the separation between the browser’s current time and server completion.

messages.text: Native controls do not make the lesson outline navigable by themselves.
Playback does not establish durable lesson completion.
A role and name are incomplete when keyboard operation and state do not stay synchronized.

options.text: Use native media controls and distinguish playback from recorded completion.
Use native media controls but leave the lesson outline outside a named region.
Use a named outline and treat browser playback as proof of server completion.
Use custom ARIA buttons whose keyboard actions do not update their exposed states.

prompt: A course player has lesson landmarks and media controls; playback state is local to the browser. Users must navigate lesson sections and control playback without confusing browser playback state with server lesson metadata. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: Keyboard users must operate preview controls, while only an authorized server action may publish the lesson.
An author previews a lesson before publishing it.

feedback.reason: An accessible name tells users what a control does; neither the name nor DOM state grants publication authority.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Preview and publish are distinct actions; the service owns permission and the UI communicates each action and result.
details.scenarioApplication: A screen-reader user can identify preview versus publish, and a denied publish response remains distinct from preview success.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A preview-only role may hide publishing controls when the user lacks permission, while the service still validates every request.
details.errorCorrection: Label preview as “Published” in the accessibility tree so users know it is ready. An accessible name tells users what a control does; neither the name nor DOM state grants publication authority.
details.transfer: If authorization changes, update available controls and keep the server as final authority.

messages.text: Preview and publication are distinct states.
Removing a control only for assistive technology creates inconsistent interfaces and does not enforce permission.
An ARIA property can communicate disabled state but cannot enforce authorization.

options.text: Expose the preview state as “Published” while the service processes the request.
Remove Publish from the accessibility tree while leaving it visible to other users.
Expose Preview and Publish separately; authorize publication on the server.
Use aria-disabled on Publish as the only check for publication permission.

prompt: An author previews a lesson before publishing it. Keyboard users must operate preview controls, while only an authorized server action may publish the lesson. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: Users must identify each notification and hear whether it became read without overwriting a newer server state.
A notification list receives a read-state update from another browser tab.

feedback.reason: A list and status provide meaning, but concurrency still requires version-aware state so a stale tab cannot reverse a newer read action.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Semantic item names and a concise status make the interaction understandable; the update protocol owns conflict resolution.
details.scenarioApplication: The changed notification is identified in the list and the announcement reflects the accepted state after concurrency checks.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: An optimistic message can be used when it is corrected on rejection and the user can distinguish pending from accepted state.
details.errorCorrection: Use a semantic list but optimistically announce “read” before the server resolves a concurrent update. A list and status provide meaning, but concurrency still requires version-aware state so a stale tab cannot reverse a newer read action.
details.transfer: When another tab wins the update, reconcile the displayed state and announce the resulting value.

messages.text: A concurrent update can reject the optimistic state, making the announcement false.
Repeating the entire list obscures which item changed.
A dot alone does not communicate read state.

options.text: Announce an item as read before its concurrent server update is accepted.
Use one live region to reread all notifications after every state change.
Show read state with a colored dot and process the server update silently.
Name each notification and announce its accepted read-state change.

prompt: A notification list receives a read-state update from another browser tab. Users must identify each notification and hear whether it became read without overwriting a newer server state. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: Keyboard users need a fast way to reach the primary feed while late panels load independently.
A streaming home renders its main feed before personalized panels arrive.

feedback.reason: The skip target should reach the primary content immediately; late panels need their own names and must not disrupt focus.

details.mechanismOrProperty: A skip link and main landmark provide direct access, while optional panels can load without blocking or moving focus.
details.scenarioApplication: The primary feed is reachable before personalization completes, and arriving panels remain identifiable in the page structure.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If recommendations are the user’s explicit destination, a second skip target can help without replacing the main feed link.
details.errorCorrection: Wait for personalized panels before rendering main, then expose each card as an application landmark. The skip target should reach the primary content immediately; late panels need their own names and must not disrupt focus.
details.transfer: When a panel appears after load, insert it without changing the active focus location.

messages.text: The primary feed needs direct navigation regardless of recommendation loading.
The main task should not wait for optional personalization.
Inserting content before active focus can move the user’s reading position unexpectedly.

options.text: Link the skip control to recommendations and leave the main feed without a heading.
Link a skip action to the early main feed and name later panels separately.
Wait for optional panels before exposing the main landmark.
Render the main feed early but insert panels before the active focus location.

prompt: A streaming home renders its main feed before personalized panels arrive. Keyboard users need a fast way to reach the primary feed while late panels load independently. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: The viewer must distinguish the event and receive a meaningful update without confusing an old date with the new one.
A shared calendar event is moved while another attendee is viewing it.

feedback.reason: The announcement should describe the accepted change, not a stale event; moving focus would interrupt the calendar task.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Headings and date/time labels establish event identity, while a version-aware update determines which change to announce.
details.scenarioApplication: The attendee can identify the changed event and hear its accepted new time without losing the current calendar position.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A visual badge may supplement the announcement if it names the same changed event and time.
details.errorCorrection: Announce every incoming event payload before checking which version is current. The announcement should describe the accepted change, not a stale event; moving focus would interrupt the calendar task.
details.transfer: When an older event update arrives late, ignore it and do not announce it as the current value.

messages.text: An older payload may arrive after a newer event and produce a false announcement.
The time change is not available to users who cannot see the badge.
A background update does not require moving the user’s focus.

options.text: Announce the accepted event version while preserving calendar focus.
Announce each event payload as it arrives, before checking its version.
Use semantic event headings but show the changed time only in a visual badge.
Move focus to the event card whenever an attendee changes its time.

prompt: A shared calendar event is moved while another attendee is viewing it. The viewer must distinguish the event and receive a meaningful update without confusing an old date with the new one. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: The approver must operate the action accessibly, while the server independently enforces authorization and audit.
A finance approval screen shows an exceptional payout request.

feedback.reason: Accessible labeling does not grant authority; server authorization and audit must remain independent requirements.

details.mechanismOrProperty: Native named buttons serve keyboard and assistive-technology users; authorization is checked by the transaction owner.
details.scenarioApplication: The approver can identify and activate the choice, and the outcome is accepted only after the server validates permission and writes audit evidence.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Hiding a control for unauthorized users can improve clarity, but the server must still reject unauthorized requests.
details.errorCorrection: Use an accessible label saying “Authorized approval” and treat that label as the permission check. Accessible labeling does not grant authority; server authorization and audit must remain independent requirements.
details.transfer: If server authorization fails, announce the rejection and leave the payout unapproved.

messages.text: An accessible name cannot grant transaction permission.
The action still needs a programmatic name for assistive technology users.
The audit contract must not depend on input modality.

options.text: Label the control “Authorized approval” and treat its accessible name as permission.
Keep server checks but expose Approve and Reject as unlabeled icon buttons.
Make approval keyboard-operable but skip audit for non-pointer activation.
Name approval actions and enforce authorization and audit on the server.

prompt: A finance approval screen shows an exceptional payout request. The approver must operate the action accessibly, while the server independently enforces authorization and audit. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: A screen-reader user needs the current result state, and an older response must not replace newer intent.
A search field sends a new request before the previous result returns.

feedback.reason: Sequence protection selects the current result; a concise status communicates its outcome without claiming that ARIA controls request ordering.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The request owner handles stale responses; the accessibility layer announces only the accepted result state.
details.scenarioApplication: The user hears which query completed and stale results cannot replace the response for the latest query.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A loading status is useful when it begins once and is followed by the final result or empty state.
details.errorCorrection: Announce every response as it arrives and let the most recent completion update the result list. Sequence protection selects the current result; a concise status communicates its outcome without claiming that ARIA controls request ordering.
details.transfer: When cancellation is unavailable, compare request sequence before committing data or announcing the result.

messages.text: An empty result is still a user-relevant outcome.
Repeated loading noise and stale labels misrepresent the displayed query.
A late older response is no longer the user’s current query.

options.text: Reject stale data but leave a no-match result without status.
Announce loading on every render while labeling old results as current.
Announce the latest query result after rejecting stale responses.
Announce every response in completion order, even after a newer query.

prompt: A search field sends a new request before the previous result returns. A screen-reader user needs the current result state, and an older response must not replace newer intent. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?

constraints: A keyboard user must search, choose a place, and read the selected place details.
A map search must remain usable when a low-powered device cannot render the map canvas.

feedback.reason: A named canvas cannot provide the complete search and selection task when it is unavailable; semantic results must be operable independently.

details.mechanismOrProperty: The search form and result list define the task interface; map rendering is supplemental.
details.scenarioApplication: Users can choose and inspect a place while the canvas is still loading or absent.
details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A map pin can remain a shortcut when keyboard users can reach the same result through the list.
details.errorCorrection: Name the canvas and make pins focusable, but leave result selection inside the map. A named canvas cannot provide the complete search and selection task when it is unavailable; semantic results must be operable independently.
details.transfer: When canvas rendering recovers, preserve the selected place and synchronize the supplemental view.

messages.text: A text alternative must remain available during map failure, not after it.
Captions cannot select a route or provide keyboard operation.
Focusable pins do not cover route selection when the canvas is delayed.

options.text: Provide route text only after the canvas finishes rendering.
Keep selectable results and directions usable while the map is delayed.
Name the canvas and expose route names only in a noninteractive caption.
Provide keyboard-focusable pins but require map dragging to choose a route.

prompt: A map search must remain usable when a low-powered device cannot render the map canvas. A keyboard user must search, choose a place, and read the selected place details. Which interface decision best meets the accessibility requirement while keeping the adjacent system responsibility explicit?
